Many traders keep large equity and mutual fund portfolios sitting idle while they put fresh cash into F&O margin.

That's capital working only once when it could work twice.

How collateral margin works:
• You pledge eligible shares or mutual fund units in your own demat account.
• Your broker gives you margin against them after a haircut, which depends on the security's risk.
• You keep ownership. Dividends and long-term growth stay with you.

What serious traders need to know:
→ Exchange rules require a cash component in F&O margin, so collateral can't replace cash completely.
→ Haircuts can change, and a falling market cuts collateral value just when you need margin most.
→ Using collateral is leverage. Size positions for the bad day, not the average day.

Used with discipline, pledging is one of the most efficient tools available to an Indian F&O trader. Used carelessly, it's how a long-term portfolio gets hurt by a short-term trade.
